headline: High: shared filesystem writes and git mutation create default-conflict and leakage risks; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower but present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b reads/writes the filesystem and processes files passed on the command line. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where attacker-controlled text from A can be fed into B as trusted instructions. The pair lacks explicit provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into files that agent_b later ingests, injection becomes actionable.
IF the two agents share a workspace or command-line handoff, B may parse A's output as directives.
mitigations: Add a strict instruction/data delimiter in shared files.
Require B to ignore any imperative language in A-produced artifacts.
Use separate directories for A and B outputs.
Manually review A outputs before B consumes them.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all inter-agent handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, learning patterns, performance metrics, and task prompts; agent_b reads selected source files and writes to the filesystem. Because B's shared state is via filesystem and A can interact through MCP/stdin-stdout, sensitive prompts or metadata can flow into B outputs in default workflows. The pairwise leakage path is plausible even without explicit secret handling overlap.
conditions: IF agent_a stores task prompts or repository metadata in shared files, agent_b can read them.
IF B writes diffs or logs into the shared workspace, A-originated sensitive context may persist.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Disable writing prompts or metadata to shared paths.
Review B output files before committing or sharing.
Rotate any exposed API keys or signatures if found in shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell commands, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can modify git state and write the filesystem, with shared state explicitly via filesystem. That is the rubric's dangerous overlap: both can mutate the same repo without locking, so concurrent edits or git corruption are plausible in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout, concurrent git writes can conflict.
IF multiple instances run simultaneously, filesystem races can corrupt edits or history.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own clone.
Serialize git operations with a lock file.
Pause one agent while the other commits.
Inspect git status before each write.
requires-engineering: add transactional edit coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces analysis through hooks/workers and MCP, while agent_b is a CLI coding assistant that applies diff-based edit proposals after user confirmation. B can treat A's output as input for edits, so an error in A can cascade into incorrect code changes unless explicitly verified. The confirmation step reduces but does not eliminate the pathway.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated summaries or plans without independent verification, errors propagate.
IF A's background analysis is stale, B may edit code based on outdated facts.
mitigations: Require B to cite source lines before editing.
Compare A outputs against the underlying files.
Use a human review step for all diffs.
Limit A to advisory output only.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between A and B.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles Ed25519 signatures and task prompts, while agent_b handles model provider API keys and selected source files. No explicit residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented, so only a limited compliance gap is visible from the profiles. Because the evidence is sparse, I avoid asserting a stronger violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent's workspace, retention and residency controls must be rechecked.
IF shared logs capture prompts or keys, compliance scope expands.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces.
Review retention settings for both agents.
Separate secret material from code files.
Document where logs are stored.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement.
